idiom_name: Iterator::fold / reduce / rfold / try_fold, plus Sum and Product
implementation_notes: Rust's fold is a trait method on every iterator: fold(init, f) consumes the iterator left to right (1.0), reduce (1.51) is the seedless form returning Option, rfold (1.27, DoubleEndedIterator) is the documented right-associative counterpart, try_fold (1.27) threads a Try/ControlFlow carrier so a fold can short-circuit on the first failure, and the Sum/Product traits (1.11) make sum()/product() the monoid spellings. Because fold takes self, elements move out of the iterator - a fold that must leave the collection usable borrows it first with iter()/iter_mut(), which also gives references instead of owned values. Prefer these methods over a hand-written loop: they compose with the adapter chain, name the direction in the method, and inline to the same machine code.
pitfalls: fold/reduce consume the iterator: the elements of a ByValue iterator are moved out, so folding a Vec's IntoIter and then needing the Vec is a borrow-checker error - and folding &T while the accumulator wants owned values forces a clone per step.
try_fold is stable but try_reduce is still a nightly-only experimental API, so the fallible seedless fold has to be written as try_fold plus an explicit Option/ControlFlow rather than as try_reduce.

A recursive fold over an enum tree (match plus Box) is one frame per level: Rust guarantees no tail-call elimination, so deep structures need an explicit stack, an iterative adapter chain or a trampoline.

variants.name: Parallel fold with rayon (ParallelIterator::fold / reduce)
variants.idiom_name: rayon::iter ParallelIterator::fold(identity, fold_op) followed by reduce(identity, op)
variants.implementation_notes: rayon extends the same vocabulary to parallel data: ParallelIterator::fold(identity, fold_op) produces a Fold adaptor that folds each split chunk independently - the documentation describes it as similar to the sequential fold except that the items may be subdivided - and reduce(identity, op) then merges the partial results, so the operations must be associative with a true identity per chunk. Use it for large, CPU-bound, genuinely associative reductions (sums, counts, histograms), keep the sequential Iterator::fold for small inputs and I/O-bound work where the split cost and pool interactions dominate, and use try_reduce/try_fold when the fold is fallible. This is a crate rather than the standard library, so it adds a dependency and a thread pool to the program's footprint.
pitfalls: Associativity and a true identity are required but unchecked: a non-associative op or a wrong identity makes the parallel result differ from the sequential one, and floating-point sums are the canonical example.

rayon runs on a work-stealing pool of its own: a fold whose closure blocks, locks or performs I/O starves the pool, and for small inputs the splitting and merging cost more than the fold itself - measure before switching.
It is an external dependency: a crate that only needs a quick reduction should not pull in thread-pool infrastructure, and the version has to be pinned like any other dependency that affects results.
